Entity.description: Data and the rules that belong to it. Survives across turns.

Control.description: Logic that realises the use case “play a turn”. Sequences the entities. Named xxxController / xxxMgr (Ch 6 slide 43).

Boundary.description: Interaction between the manager (actor) and the system. Named xxxUI (Ch 6 slide 43).

Supporting.description: Not E/C/B on their own: roles, enums, errors, a utility and the launcher.

added_classes.how_found: We walked through §3.2 and asked “who runs steps 1 to 6 in this order and talks to the CLI?” No noun owned that.
added_classes.why: §2.2 says rules belong in domain and control objects, not the UI. Someone has to sequence them.

added_classes.how_found: Steps 1, 4 and 5 need no manager input. In a first draft they sat in GameController, which then handled UI calls, the loop and rules: three reasons to change.
added_classes.why: SRP. Same idea as FASMgr handing fingerprint logic to FingerprintMgr (Ch 7). The automatic rules can be tested without a console.

added_classes.how_found: While writing GameController.assignTask() we needed to ask for input and show output. Calling Scanner directly would tie the rules to the console.
added_classes.why: DIP: the high-level controller depends on an abstraction. A GUI or a scripted test UI can replace ConsoleUI without touching the controller.

added_classes.how_found: The only place that touches Scanner and System.out.
added_classes.why: Keeps the brief’s rule that the UI only collects decisions and displays state.

added_classes.how_found: Revenue, served count, departures and average satisfaction had no owner in the noun list.
added_classes.why: Putting them in Cashier would mix “take a payment” with “report results” (low cohesion).

added_classes.how_found: The victory check needs three targets together.
added_classes.why: Targets can change (difficulty settings) without editing the game loop (OCP).

added_classes.how_found: Every fixed number in §2.1 was scattered across classes on the first pass.
added_classes.why: One place for the base setting gives reproducible runs and one place to change.

added_classes.how_found: “One customer at the start of turns 1, 4, 7 …” is a schedule, not a customer property.
added_classes.why: Holds a factory per turn (RegularCustomer::new, a Java 8 method reference). New customer kinds register here instead of in the turn logic.

added_classes.how_found: Verb analysis showed the same rule three times: “one task / one unit / one payment per turn”.
added_classes.why: Write the once-per-turn rule once; subclasses inherit it.

added_classes.how_found: Verb analysis split staff into two kinds: Waiter and Chef take the manager’s choices, the Cashier acts automatically.
added_classes.why: A perform() in Staff would force Cashier to fake or throw (an LSP problem like Tutorial 8 Q3). A small role interface solves it (ISP). The controller loops over a List<Assignable>.

added_classes.how_found: Designing the CLI prompt: the choice “seat 3” has to reach the Waiter without the UI checking whether it is legal.
§3.4: an invalid choice must explain why and let the manager choose again without using the task.
added_classes.why: A checked custom exception (Ch 4): the compiler forces GameController to handle it. The staff member is marked as acted only after success.

added_classes.how_found: Step 5 needs “waiting or seated and not served”; step 4 needs eating and READY_TO_PAY.
added_classes.why: Status checks live inside Customer as isAwaitingService(), canPay(turn), so callers do not compare statuses themselves.
One formatting method, so no class prints money in its own way.

added_classes.how_found: Something must create the objects and connect them.
added_classes.why: Composition root (Ch 2 “application class”). It injects ConsoleUI into GameController (DIP).

assumptions.rule: Customer #n orders menu item (n − 1) mod 3 from [Salad, Burger, Pasta]. So the six arrivals order Salad, Burger, Pasta, Salad, Burger, Pasta. The choice is shown when the order is taken.
Step 1 arrivals run before the start-of-turn display, so the manager sees the customer who just arrived.
The manager picks which queued customer to seat. The lowest-numbered free table is used, since tables are identical.
An order takes its customer’s id, so “cook 3” means customer #3’s order.
Eating updates run first, then the Cashier. The Cashier only charges a customer whose READY_TO_PAY turn is earlier than the current turn.
